promptText: What fundamentally distinguishes an "agent" from a single tool-calling chat request?
options: An agent must always use exactly three tools per task

An agent wraps the decide/act/observe cycle in a repeated loop until the task is complete or a limit is reached, whereas a single tool-calling request makes one model call that may invoke one tool and return
An agent never produces a final natural-language answer
An agent requires a multi-agent architecture by definition
explanation: The defining feature of an agent is the repeated observe-think-act cycle, not merely the presence of tools — a bare tool-calling API answers one question, an agent loops until done.

promptText: What does ReAct stand for, and what does interleaving an explicit "thought" with each action accomplish?
options: Reactive Architecture; it makes the agent respond faster by skipping reasoning
Reasoning + Acting; writing reasoning out as text before acting measurably improves the chosen action's quality and creates a debuggable audit trail
Recursive Action; it lets the agent call itself as a sub-agent
Retrieval + Action; it only applies to RAG-based agents
explanation: ReAct interleaves an explicit Thought, an Action (tool call), and an Observation (tool result) in a repeated loop — writing the reasoning out improves decision quality and gives engineers a breadcrumb trail explaining why the agent acted.

promptText: What concrete engineering controls prevent an agent loop from running unbounded in production?
options: A carefully worded system prompt telling the model to stop when it feels done
A hard maximum iteration count and a maximum cumulative token/cost budget enforced in the orchestrating code, independent of what the model "thinks" it should do
Relying entirely on the model's own hasToolCalls() output with no other safeguard
Increasing the context window so the model never forgets its goal
explanation: Production code never trusts the model's own 'I'm done' signal alone — it enforces a hard ceiling in deterministic code, because a model can get stuck oscillating between actions without ever emitting a clean stop signal.

promptText: What structurally distinguishes a "stateless" agent worker process from a "stateful" one?
options: Stateless workers cannot call any tools

A stateless worker holds no session-specific memory between invocations — every call receives the full context it needs and any instance can serve any request — while a stateful worker keeps an in-memory session tied to a specific process across turns
Stateful workers are always faster to scale horizontally than stateless ones
There is no meaningful difference for agent architectures
explanation: Statelessness lets any instance behind a load balancer serve any request, which is why production agent platforms generally prefer it — stateful sessions require sticky routing and complicate failover.

promptText: What is "checkpointing" in the context of long-running agents, and why does it matter architecturally?
options: Periodically restarting the underlying model to clear its cache

Persisting the agent's full trajectory state (messages, pending plan, intermediate results) to durable storage at defined points, so a crash or redeploy mid-trajectory doesn't silently lose the entire in-flight task
A billing feature that caps the maximum tokens per request
A technique exclusive to multi-agent systems, never used for a single agent
explanation: Without checkpointing, an infrastructure restart or crash mid-trajectory silently loses all in-flight work; checkpoints also enable audit and mid-trajectory human review since they are inspectable snapshots rather than transient RAM.

promptText: What does an "orchestrator" agent do differently from a "worker" agent in a hub-and-spoke topology?
options: The orchestrator calls domain tools directly while workers never do

The orchestrator holds overall task state, decides which worker to invoke next, and assembles results, typically without calling domain tools itself; a worker is a narrower specialist that receives a bounded sub-task and returns a result
Workers always run on more capable models than the orchestrator
There is no structural difference; the terms are interchangeable
explanation: The orchestrator is the hub holding shared context and routing logic; workers are focused spokes that can be added or replaced independently without visibility into the rest of the system's state.

promptText: If each decision step in an agent trajectory succeeds independently with probability p, and a task requires n sequential correct decisions with no error-correction between them, roughly what happens to overall trajectory success as n grows, and what design response follows?
options: Success probability stays constant at p regardless of n, so no special design response is needed

Success probability degrades roughly as p^n (e.g., 95% per step drops to ~60% by step ten), which motivates breaking long chains into shorter, independently verifiable segments or inserting a reflection/verification step
Success probability increases with n because the model learns from its own earlier steps
This only matters for multi-agent systems, not for a single agent's ReAct loop
explanation: This is the chapter's core compounding-probability argument: small per-step reliability gains have outsized, compounding payoff on long trajectories, which is why Plan-and-Execute, reflection, and decomposition all exist.

promptText: Compare ReAct and Plan-and-Execute architectures. When would Plan-and-Execute be preferred?
options: ReAct is always preferred because it never requires a termination check

Plan-and-Execute is preferred for longer tasks or when a human should review/approve an explicit plan before any action is taken, trading some adaptability for a more inspectable, controllable trajectory versus ReAct's step-by-step improvisation
Plan-and-Execute cannot be combined with tool calling at all
ReAct and Plan-and-Execute produce identical trajectories in every case
explanation: ReAct decides one step at a time with no global plan, which is fine for short exploratory tasks but risky for long ones since a flawed early step has no global view correcting it; Plan-and-Execute produces an upfront plan a human can review.

promptText: What structurally distinguishes a graph-based agent architecture (e.g., LangGraph's philosophy) from a conversation-based one (e.g., AutoGen's philosophy)?
options: Graph-based architectures cannot use tools at all

A graph-based architecture declares control flow explicitly and statically as nodes and edges over a typed shared state; a conversation-based architecture lets control flow emerge implicitly from what agents say in a shared chat transcript, discovered only at runtime
Conversation-based architectures are always cheaper to run
The two approaches are functionally identical, differing only in library name
explanation: Because a graph's state and transitions are declared up front, checkpointing simply means persisting that typed state at a node boundary; conversation-based control flow is more flexible but harder to statically bound or audit.

promptText: What requirement would push a design toward a single-agent architecture rather than multi-agent, even though multi-agent is often presented as more sophisticated?
options: The task fits comfortably in one context window without competing responsibilities, and latency/cost budgets are tight, since multi-agent multiplies the number of sequential model calls
The task involves reading any external content whatsoever
The organization has more than one engineering team available
The task requires calling more than one tool
explanation: Multi-agent is a cost paid for decomposition benefits (focused prompts, parallelism, fault isolation); if the task doesn't genuinely need that decomposition, the added latency and cost are pure overhead — single-agent should be the default, not the exception requiring justification.

promptText: Why does a state machine (or graph-based) architecture make checkpoint-resume more natural than a plain imperative loop?
options: Because state machines cannot fail, so there is nothing to recover from

Because the graph already defines discrete node boundaries and an explicit, typed state object flowing between them, so a checkpoint is simply persisting that object; a plain loop has no such natural seams, since state is scattered across local variables and call-stack position
Because imperative code always runs faster than a graph-based implementation
Because state machines eliminate the need for any tool-execution layer
explanation: An ad hoc conversation history or scattered local variables force you to retrofit an explicit state representation after the fact; a graph's typed state schema names every field the graph depends on up front.

promptText: Compare a hub-and-spoke (orchestrator + workers) topology to a peer-to-peer multi-agent topology at the structural level.
options: Hub-and-spoke concentrates task-level state in one inspectable place at the cost of a potential central bottleneck; peer-to-peer removes that bottleneck but makes it structurally harder to answer 'what is the overall state of this task right now' since no single component holds that view
Peer-to-peer always requires fewer total model calls than hub-and-spoke
Hub-and-spoke cannot support parallel execution of workers under any circumstance
The two topologies have identical failure-isolation properties
explanation: The hub becomes a single point to inspect and checkpoint but also a potential bottleneck; peer-to-peer better fits workflows without a natural central authority but requires reconstructing overall state by tracing messages across every peer.

promptText: How does "durable execution" (Temporal-style) differ architecturally from typical agent-loop checkpointing that a developer explicitly triggers?
options: Durable execution and manual checkpointing are the same technique with different marketing names

Typical checkpointing persists state snapshots the developer explicitly decides when and what to save; durable execution frameworks re-execute the workflow function from the top on resume, using a recorded event history to deterministically skip already-completed steps by replaying recorded results, in exchange for imposing stricter constraints on what code can do
Durable execution never requires any recorded event history
Manual checkpointing always provides stronger exactly-once guarantees than durable execution
explanation: Durable execution frameworks let developers write ordinary-looking sequential code while the framework guarantees exactly-once effects and crash recoverability underneath, at the cost of restricting arbitrary non-deterministic calls outside declared 'activities.'

promptText: According to the chapter, what is the highest-leverage architectural decision a staff engineer should get right early in an agent platform's life, and why is it uniquely expensive to change later?
options: The choice of which multi-agent framework to adopt, because switching frameworks always requires a full rewrite

The state representation — what an agent's state is, how it's serialized, and the transient/durable boundary — because every other decision (checkpointing, resumability, hand-offs, tracing, versioning) is built on top of assuming a particular state shape, and changing it after production trajectories are checkpointed requires migrating or abandoning historical data
The specific vendor hosting the underlying foundation model, since model choice cannot be abstracted behind an interface
The naming convention used for tool functions, since renaming a tool always breaks every existing integration irreversibly
explanation: Tool interfaces or even graph-vs-conversation control flow are comparatively cheap to revisit later since they can be swapped behind stable boundaries, but a state schema underlies every other architectural mechanism and is a much higher-stakes retrofit once real trajectories are checkpointed under it.

promptText: A system needs to support both a fast, cheap triage agent and a slow, expensive deep-investigation agent, choosing between them per request. What architecture does the chapter recommend?
options: Always run both agents on every request and return whichever finishes first

Put a lightweight router in front (a rule, a small model call, or the triage agent's own low-confidence signal) that only escalates to the deep path when warranted, and design the deep-investigation agent to accept the triage agent's partial findings as input rather than starting from zero
Never allow escalation mid-trajectory; each request must commit to one tier upfront with no ability to switch
Route every request through the deep-investigation agent, since triage tiers add unnecessary complexity
explanation: Escalating mid-trajectory without discarding triage's prior work avoids waste, and tracking escalation rate as a first-class metric reveals whether the triage tier is well-calibrated or effectively dead weight.
